summary: This Dockerfile creates a Ubuntu container with ripgrep (a fast search tool) and zsh shell, pre-configured with custom functions for finding TODO comments and environment variable references across a project. It also sets up a demo project with sample code files to showcase how these search tools work, then drops you into an interactive shell when the container starts.

explanations.3: This tells the installer to not prompt for user input during package installation, which is necessary in Docker where there's no interactive terminal.
explanations.6: The --no-install-recommends flag tells apt to skip extra packages that aren't strictly needed, keeping the container smaller.
explanations.11: After installing packages, we delete the apt cache to reduce the final image size since we won't need to install anything else.
explanations.14: The printf with '%s\n' outputs each argument on its own line—this is a way to write multi-line content into a file when you can't use heredocs in Docker.
explanations.30: The > redirects all that printf output into the .ripgreprc file, which ripgrep will read for configuration settings.
explanations.33: We create the directory structure ahead of time so the RUN commands that write files into it won't fail.
explanations.38: The ${1:-.} syntax means 'use the first argument if provided, otherwise default to the current directory'.
explanations.47: [[ -z "${var}" ]] checks if the variable is empty; if it is, the function prints usage info and exits with error code 1.
explanations.55: This line sources (loads) all custom zsh functions from the fns folder whenever a new shell starts.
explanations.60: The >> appends to the existing .zshrc file instead of overwriting it, so we keep whatever was already there.
explanations.79: We initialize a git repository in the demo folder so the sample files have git history, making the demo more realistic.
explanations.80: The -c flags set temporary git config values just for this one command so we can commit without a pre-configured user.
explanations.90: The -i flag makes the shell interactive and -l makes it a login shell, so it reads your configuration files when it starts.
